events.title: THEATRE l I'd Love to Have You for Dinner
events.venue: Black Box - 2357 Caniff Hamtramck, MI 48212 - Entrance in the rear
events.summary: I'd Love to Have You For Dinner Psychological Thriller 2 Acts w/ Intermission 1 Hour 40 Minutes IMPORTANT NOTE: This show contains extreme violence and gore. Viewer discretion is advised. Two lovebirds, Ania and Charles, meet for their first-and-three-quarters date: a home cooked meal. But there is a secret at the table: one of them eats people. The other, of course, is fully aware, because the one who eats people – Ania – is an ancient vampire, while the other – Charles – hunts and eats vampires alive. When these forces – life, and unlife – go for each other’s throats, who will go home with a full stomach? This two act, four-course horror/thriller highlights legacy, cannibalism, the inevitability of personal failure, and the complex moral nature of predation in all its incarnations. Starring: Celah Convis as Ania Komorowski Alex Aho as Charles Marlene Goss as Lady Michele Harte, Director and Writer Julia Lebrell, Stage Manager Max Wray, Marketing

events.title: Kathleen Beck, carillon
events.summary: Kathleen Beck performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.title: Everything I Want to Do In a Show | A One Woman Show
events.summary: Hi, I'm Heather Sejnow. You may remember me from such things as that Christmas Commercial for a toy store that gets played every year near St. Claire Shores; hosting shows at the Senate or Redford Theatre as dead celebrities or film characters; or living in Chicago for a short while to do Second City, iO, and then hop back to Detroit to perform at Go Comedy and Planet Ant. I've even nabbed the title of the only female stand up impressionist in the state of Michigan ( that I know of) . I haven't been on a real theatrical performance stage in a while and I'm about to turn 40. So for my mid-life crisis I'm putting on a show of "Everything I Want to Do in a Show". It's campy, crazy, and heartfelt. Most importantly, it's a love letter to everyone I've met and all the vessels of creativity I've learned along the way. Oh! And it's interactive, NSFW, and there will be some prizes for attendees. So come join me on a wild ride filled with puppets, impressions, burlesque, song, dance, and even Shakespeare. It's definitely... "Everything".

events.title: Probing Chemistry Without Pushing It: An Electrochemical View
events.summary: For more than a century, electrochemical kinetics have been measured largely by driving reactions away from equilibrium, most famously through Tafel analysis. This works well when a single kinetic barrier dominates, but becomes much harder to interpret when several barriers contribute or when the reaction is so fast that moving away from equilibrium immediately brings in mass transport. We recently discovered that equilibrium current fluctuations offer a way around both problems. Because the system is not being driven, the fluctuations report directly on the underlying microscopic exchange processes, allowing intrinsic kinetic information to be extracted without the usual convolution with diffusion and with the possibility of resolving more than one characteristic timescale. We are now extending this idea to adsorption and desorption at catalytic surfaces which are the elementary steps often controlling electrocatalytic reactions but are difficult to measure independently. The fluctuation magnitude and autocorrelation function provide access to both surface occupancy and characteristic adsorption/desorption timescales. As we move into highly concentrated electrolytes, including the water-in-salt regime, we observe striking changes in these dynamics. The second part of the talk carries the same idea into a very different environment: using electrochemistry not simply to drive a process, but to uncover the thermodynamics and kinetics hidden within it. Here, the system is a biomolecular condensate formed by liquidliquid phase separation. The classic Miller–Urey experiments used electrical energy to drive chemical transformations relevant to the origins of life; in our case, we use electrical potential primarily as a probe of chemistry inside a highly concentrated biological phase. We recently found that entering a biomolecular condensate can fundamentally reshape the thermodynamic landscape of a redox reaction, an effect we probed by combining electrochemistry with OPTIR spectroscopy. One consequence is that a reaction that is nonspontaneous in ordinary aqueous solution may become spontaneous inside the condensate. We are now turning from thermodynamics to kinetics, asking whether the intrinsic rate constant itself also changes. This distinction is essential because reactions can appear much faster inside condensates simply because reactants partition strongly into the dense phase, without necessarily becoming intrinsically more reactive. More broadly, these studies ask how much of chemical reactivity is determined not only by the reacting molecules themselves, but by the microscopic environment in which the reaction occurs.

events.title: Awakening the Dragon–Showcasing the Building and Performance of an Asian Icon
events.summary: Experience a curated experience of the imaginary, featuring a lightly sci-fi, magnificent work of art--the LRCCS Fortune and Longevity Dragon, a 25-ft long, Asian-inspired full-body dragon sculpture for use in the traditional "dragon dance" crafted by renowned international artist Zhen Guo with U-M faculty arts lecturer Raymond Wetzel, artist Jeri Rosenberg, students, and volunteers The exhibition highlights the story of the dragon's fabrication and its impact on community.. An iconic symbol of inclusivity, strength, and courage, this newly imagined U-M dragon, with its futuristic flair, technological creativity and sustainable materials, invites students and the entire community to re-envision a classic cultural symbol for contemporary times. Presented by the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies. This project was made possible by grants from the University of Michigan Arts Initiative and the Office of the Provost, Global Engagement. Additional funding was provided by ArtsEngine, Center for World Performance Studies, Stearns Collection of Musical Instruments, and U.S. Department of Education. featuredEvents.experienceId: experience:["ann arbor","east hall","topology seminar tight surgeries on torus knots"]
featuredEvents.title: Topology seminar: Tight surgeries on torus knots
featuredEvents.summary: This seminar explores the classification of tight contact structures on surgeries along torus knots, a significant advancement in understanding these complex mathematical spaces. The discussion will delve into the role of Heegaard Floer invariants and contact geometry in this classification, offering insights into advanced topological concepts.

evidence.description: Abstract: We give a complete classification of tight contact structures on every surgery along torus knots, which provides the first such classification on an infinite family of non-trivial knots and makes progress on the project of understanding tight contact structures on Seifert fibered spaces.

featuredEvents.experienceId: experience:["ann arbor","west hall","neural simulation based inference for scalable high fidelity spatial modeling"]
featuredEvents.title: Neural simulation-based inference for scalable, high-fidelity spatial modeling
featuredEvents.summary: Explore a paradigm shift in statistical science using neural simulation-based inference. This seminar delves into training neural networks with statistical models for faster, more accurate inference, particularly in complex spatial and spatio-temporal statistics. Discover its potential for scaling up and increasing fidelity in real-world applications.

evidence.description: Neural simulation-based inference is a recent paradigm shift in statistical science that uses simulations from a statistical model to train a neural network for statistical inference.
